prompt: Give all possible representations of $2022$ as a sum of at least two consecutive positive integers and prove that these are the only representations.

solutions.title: Factor $2\cdot2022$
solutions.body:
Suppose $2022=M+(M+1)+\cdots+N$ with $1\le M<N$. Then
$$2022=\frac{N(N+1)}2-\frac{(M-1)M}2=\frac{(N+M)(N-M+1)}{2},$$
so
$$(N+M)(N-M+1)=4044=2^2\cdot3\cdot337 .$$
Put $u=N+M$ and $v=N-M+1$ (the number of terms). Then $v\ge2$, $u>v$ (since $M\ge1$), and $u+v=2N+1$ is odd, so $u$ and $v$ have **opposite parity**. Conversely, any factorisation $4044=uv$ with $u>v\ge2$ of opposite parity gives $N=\frac{u+v-1}2$, $M=\frac{u-v+1}2\ge1$, a valid representation.

The divisors of $4044$ are $1,2,3,4,6,12,337,674,1011,1348,2022,4044$. The factorisations $uv$ with $u>v\ge2$ are
$$2022\cdot2,\quad1348\cdot3,\quad1011\cdot4,\quad674\cdot6,\quad337\cdot12 .$$
In $2022\cdot2$ and $674\cdot6$ both factors are even, so they are excluded. The other three give:

* $u=1348$, $v=3$: $N=675$, $M=673$: $\;2022=673+674+675$.
* $u=1011$, $v=4$: $N=507$, $M=504$: $\;2022=504+505+506+507$.
* $u=337$, $v=12$: $N=174$, $M=163$: $\;2022=163+164+\cdots+174$.

These are the only representations. ∎

solutions.title: Average times number of terms
solutions.body:
A sum of $k\ge2$ consecutive integers starting at $M$ equals $k\cdot\big(M+\frac{k-1}2\big)$.

* If $k$ is odd, $k$ must divide $2022=2\cdot3\cdot337$, and the middle term is $2022/k$. The odd divisors $k\ge2$ are $3,337,1011$. $k=3$ gives middle term $674$, i.e. $673+674+675$; $k=337$ gives middle term $6$ and first term $6-168<1$, impossible; $k=1011$ gives middle term $2$, impossible.
* If $k$ is even, the average $M+\frac{k-1}{2}$ is $\frac{j}{2}$ with $j=2M+k-1$ odd, so $kj=4044$; positivity of $M=\frac{j-k+1}2$ means $j>k$. The odd divisors $j$ of $4044$ are $1,3,337,1011$, giving $k=4044/j\in\{4044,1348,12,4\}$; only $k=12$ ($j=337$) and $k=4$ ($j=1011$) satisfy $k<j$. They give $M=\frac{337-12+1}2=163$ (twelve terms $163,\dots,174$) and $M=\frac{1011-4+1}2=504$ (four terms $504,\dots,507$).

So there are exactly three representations.

prompt: Let $A$ and $B$ be the two foci of an ellipse and let $P$ be a point on this ellipse. Prove that the focal radii of $P$ (that is, the segments $\overline{AP}$ and $\overline{BP}$) form equal angles with the tangent to the ellipse at $P$.
answer: The external bisector $\ell$ of $\angle APB$ meets the ellipse only at $P$ (reflect $A$ in $\ell$ to $A'$; for $Q\ne P$ on $\ell$, $QA+QB=QA'+QB>A'B=PA+PB$), so $\ell$ is the tangent.

solutions.title: Reflect one focus in the external bisector
solutions.body:
Let $2a=PA+PB$ be the constant sum defining the ellipse; $2a>AB$. Let $e_1,e_2$ be the unit vectors from $P$ towards $A$ and $B$. They are not opposite (that would put $P$ on segment $AB$, giving $PA+PB=AB<2a$), so $u=e_1+e_2\ne0$. Let $\ell$ be the line through $P$ perpendicular to $u$ — the external bisector of angle $APB$ — and let $w$ be a unit direction vector of $\ell$.

**$\ell$ makes equal angles with $PA$ and $PB$.** Since $w\perp u$, $e_2\cdot w=(u-e_1)\cdot w=-e_1\cdot w$. So the angle between ray $PA$ and the ray of $\ell$ in direction $w$ equals the angle between ray $PB$ and the opposite ray of $\ell$ (direction $-w$).

**Reflection.** Reflection $\rho$ in $\ell$ sends a vector $v$ (based at $P$) to $v-2\frac{v\cdot u}{|u|^2}u$. Since $e_1\cdot u=1+e_1\cdot e_2$ and $|u|^2=2+2e_1\cdot e_2$, we get $\rho(e_1)=e_1-u=-e_2$. Hence $A'=\rho(A)=P-PA\cdot e_2$ lies on line $PB$, on the other side of $P$ from $B$, and
$$A'B=A'P+PB=PA+PB=2a .$$

**$\ell$ is the tangent at $P$.** Let $Q\in\ell$, $Q\ne P$. Since reflection in $\ell$ fixes $Q$, $QA=QA'$. The line $A'B$ meets $\ell$ only at $P$ (it is not contained in $\ell$, as $e_2\cdot u=1+e_1\cdot e_2>0$), so $Q$ is not on segment $A'B$ and the triangle inequality is strict:
$$QA+QB=QA'+QB>A'B=2a .$$
So $Q$ is not on the ellipse: $\ell$ meets the ellipse only at $P$. In coordinates where the ellipse is $\frac{x^2}{\alpha^2}+\frac{y^2}{\beta^2}=1$ and $P=(x_0,y_0)$, a line $P+s(p,r)$ meets it where
$$\Big(\frac{p^2}{\alpha^2}+\frac{r^2}{\beta^2}\Big)s^2+2\Big(\frac{x_0p}{\alpha^2}+\frac{y_0r}{\beta^2}\Big)s=0,$$
which has a second root $s\ne0$ unless $\frac{x_0p}{\alpha^2}+\frac{y_0r}{\beta^2}=0$, i.e. unless the line is the tangent $\frac{x_0x}{\alpha^2}+\frac{y_0y}{\beta^2}=1$. Hence $\ell$ is the tangent at $P$, and by the first step the focal radii make equal angles with it. ∎

solutions.title: Gradient of the distance sum
solutions.body:
Let $F(X)=|X-A|+|X-B|$; the ellipse is the level set $F=2a$. Away from the foci $F$ is differentiable with
$$\nabla F(X)=\frac{X-A}{|X-A|}+\frac{X-B}{|X-B|} .$$
At $P$ this is $-(e_1+e_2)$, where $e_1,e_2$ are the unit vectors from $P$ to $A$ and $B$; it is nonzero because $e_1\ne-e_2$ (see the first solution). So the ellipse is a smooth curve near $P$ and its tangent at $P$ is perpendicular to $e_1+e_2$. For a unit tangent vector $w$ we then have $e_1\cdot w=-e_2\cdot w$, i.e.
$$\cos\angle(e_1,w)=\cos\angle(e_2,-w):$$
the focal radius $PA$ makes with one ray of the tangent the same angle as $PB$ makes with the other ray. ∎

prompt: Find all positive integers $a,b,c,d$, and $n$ satisfying $n^a+n^b+n^c=n^d$ and prove that these are the only such solutions.
answer: Either $n=3$ and $a=b=c=k-1$, $d=k$ ($k\ge2$), or $n=2$ and $\{a,b,c\}=\{k-2,k-2,k-1\}$ as a multiset, $d=k$ ($k\ge3$).

solutions.title: Divide by $n^d$
solutions.body:
By symmetry assume $a\le b\le c$ (at the end, permute). $n=1$ gives $3=1$, so $n\ge2$. Then $n^d>n^c$, so $d\ge c+1$ and all of $a-d,b-d,c-d$ are $\le-1$. Dividing by $n^d$,
$$n^{a-d}+n^{b-d}+n^{c-d}=1,\qquad\text{each term}\le\frac1n .$$
So $1\le\frac3n$, i.e. $n\le3$.

* **$n=3$:** equality $1=\frac33$ forces every term to be $\frac13$: $a=b=c=d-1$. Indeed $3\cdot3^{k-1}=3^k$.
* **$n=2$:** if $c-d\le-2$, all three terms are $\le\frac14$ and the sum is $\le\frac34<1$; so $c=d-1$ and $2^{a-d}+2^{b-d}=\frac12$. If $b-d=-1$ the left side exceeds $\frac12$, so $b-d\le-2$, and then both terms are $\le\frac14$ with sum $\frac12$, forcing $a-d=b-d=-2$. Indeed $2^{k-2}+2^{k-2}+2^{k-1}=2^{k-1}+2^{k-1}=2^k$.

**Answer.** All solutions are: $n=3$, $a=b=c=k-1$, $d=k$ for any $k\ge2$; and $n=2$, $d=k$, with $(a,b,c)$ a permutation of $(k-2,k-2,k-1)$ for any $k\ge3$ (positivity of $a,b,c$ gives the bounds on $k$). ∎

solutions.title: Base-$n$ carrying
solutions.body:
Again assume $a\le b\le c$ and $n\ge2$. Write the left side in base $n$.

If $a<b$, then $n^a+n^b+n^c=n^a(1+n^{b-a}+n^{c-a})$ and the cofactor $1+n^{b-a}+n^{c-a}\equiv1\pmod n$ is not a power of $n$ greater than $1$; but $n^d/n^a$ is such a power. So $a=b$, and the sum is $2n^a+n^c$.

* If $a=b=c$: $3n^a=n^d$ forces $n=3$, $d=a+1$.
* If $a=b<c$: $2n^a+n^c=n^a(2+n^{c-a})$, so $2+n^{c-a}$ must be a power of $n$ greater than $n^{c-a}$, hence at least $n^{c-a+1}$. Then $2\ge n^{c-a}(n-1)\ge n(n-1)$, which forces $n=2$ and $c-a=1$, giving $2^{a+1}+2^{a+1}=2^{a+2}$, i.e. $d=a+2$.

This reproduces the families in the first solution.

prompt: Calculate the exact value of the series $$\sum_{n=2}^\infty\big(\log(n^3+1)-\log(n^3-1)\big)$$ and provide justification.

solutions.title: Telescoping product
solutions.body:
Here $\log$ is the natural logarithm. The partial sums are logarithms of finite products:
$$S_N=\sum_{n=2}^N\log\frac{n^3+1}{n^3-1}=\log\prod_{n=2}^N\frac{(n+1)(n^2-n+1)}{(n-1)(n^2+n+1)} .$$
Both parts telescope:
$$\prod_{n=2}^N\frac{n+1}{n-1}=\frac{3\cdot4\cdots(N+1)}{1\cdot2\cdots(N-1)}=\frac{N(N+1)}{2},$$
and since $(n+1)^2-(n+1)+1=n^2+n+1$, the numerator of each factor $\frac{n^2-n+1}{n^2+n+1}$ cancels the previous denominator:
$$\prod_{n=2}^N\frac{n^2-n+1}{n^2+n+1}=\frac{2^2-2+1}{N^2+N+1}=\frac{3}{N^2+N+1}.$$
Hence
$$S_N=\log\frac{3N(N+1)}{2(N^2+N+1)}\xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{}\log\frac32,$$
by continuity of $\log$. (The official solution writes the two partial products as $\frac12\cdot\frac{N+1}{N-1}$ and $3\cdot\frac{N^2-N+1}{N^2+N+1}$; these are slips, but their limits $\frac12$ and $3$ happen to have the same product $\frac32$.)

**Answer: $\ln\dfrac32\approx0.4055$.**

prompt: Let $A$ be an invertible $n\times n$ matrix with complex entries. Suppose that for each positive integer $m$, there exists a positive integer $k_m$ and an $n\times n$ invertible matrix $B_m$ such that $A^{k_mm}=B_mAB_m^{-1}$. Show that all eigenvalues of $A$ are equal to $1$.
answer: Similar matrices have the same eigenvalues, so $\{\lambda_i^{k_mm}\}=\{\lambda_i\}$ as multisets; pigeonhole makes each $\lambda_i$ a root of unity, and taking $m$ a common order gives $\{\lambda_i\}=\{1,\dots,1\}$.

solutions.title: Eigenvalue multisets
solutions.body:
Let $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ be the eigenvalues of $A$ with multiplicity; all are nonzero since $A$ is invertible. Triangularise $A=UTU^{-1}$ with $T$ upper triangular (Schur); then $A^N=UT^NU^{-1}$ and $T^N$ has diagonal $\lambda_i^N$, so the eigenvalues of $A^N$ are $\lambda_1^N,\dots,\lambda_n^N$. Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial. Hence, writing $N_m=k_mm$, for every $m$
$$\{\lambda_1^{N_m},\dots,\lambda_n^{N_m}\}=\{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\}\quad\text{as multisets.}$$

**Each $\lambda_i$ is a root of unity.** Since $N_m\ge m$, the set $\{N_m:m\ge1\}$ is infinite. Fix $i$. For every $m$, $\lambda_i^{N_m}$ belongs to the finite set $\{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\}$; by the pigeonhole principle there are $m,m'$ with $N_m\ne N_{m'}$ and $\lambda_i^{N_m}=\lambda_i^{N_{m'}}$. As $\lambda_i\ne0$, $\lambda_i^{|N_m-N_{m'}|}=1$.

**Conclusion.** Let $L$ be a positive integer with $\lambda_i^L=1$ for all $i$ (e.g. the product of the orders). Taking $m=L$, $N_L=k_LL$ is a multiple of $L$, so $\lambda_i^{N_L}=1$ for all $i$. The multiset identity gives $\{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\}=\{1,\dots,1\}$: every eigenvalue of $A$ equals $1$. ∎

prompt: Let $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be a function whose second derivative is continuous. Suppose that $f$ and $f''$ are bounded. Show that $f'$ is also bounded.
answer: Taylor: $f(x+1)=f(x)+f'(x)+\tfrac12f''(\xi)$, so $|f'(x)|\le2\sup|f|+\tfrac12\sup|f''|$. (Or: a large $f'(x_0)$ stays large on an interval and makes $f$ change too much.)

solutions.title: Large derivative forces a large change of $f$
solutions.body:
Let $M>0$ with $|f(x)|\le M$ and $|f''(x)|\le M$ for all $x$, and put $N=2\sqrt2\,M$. We show $|f'(x_0)|\le N$ for every $x_0$.

Suppose $f'(x_0)>N$. Let $\delta=\frac{N}{2M}$. For $x\in[x_0-\delta,x_0]$, the mean value theorem applied to $f'$ (with $|f''|\le M$) gives
$$f'(x)\ge f'(x_0)-M(x_0-x)>N-M\delta=\frac N2 .$$
Applying the mean value theorem to $f$ on $[x_0-\delta,x_0]$, for some $\xi$ in this interval,
$$f(x_0)-f(x_0-\delta)=f'(\xi)\,\delta>\frac N2\cdot\frac{N}{2M}=\frac{N^2}{4M}=2M .$$
But $|f(x_0)-f(x_0-\delta)|\le|f(x_0)|+|f(x_0-\delta)|\le2M$ — a contradiction. So $f'(x_0)\le N$. Applying the same argument to $-f$ (which satisfies the same bounds) gives $f'(x_0)\ge-N$. Hence $|f'|\le2\sqrt2\,M$ everywhere, and $f'$ is bounded. ∎

solutions.title: Taylor's formula with one step
solutions.body:
Let $|f|\le M_0$ and $|f''|\le M_2$. For any $x$, Taylor's theorem with Lagrange remainder (valid since $f$ is twice differentiable) gives some $\xi\in(x,x+1)$ with
$$f(x+1)=f(x)+f'(x)+\tfrac12f''(\xi).$$
Hence
$$|f'(x)|=\Big|f(x+1)-f(x)-\tfrac12f''(\xi)\Big|\le2M_0+\tfrac12M_2 .$$
So $f'$ is bounded. (Optimising the step $h$ instead of $1$ gives Landau's inequality $|f'|\le2\sqrt{M_0M_2}$.) ∎
